The salary and prestige are better, but the emphasis on prosperous patients and professional display deepens his dissatisfaction. An opportunity finally takes Martin and Leora to New York's McGurk Institute, where Gottlieb is now a leading figure. Martin returns to bacteriology and finds a sympathetic colleague in the fiercely independent Terry Wickett. Institute life, however, has its own ambitions, factions, and pressures to announce results. Martin begins investigating a substance that destroys bacteria and comes to understand it as a bacteriophage. Gottlieb urges restraint and exact proof while others recognize the discovery's possible medical and reputational value. For the first time Martin has the facilities to pursue the scientific life he imagined, along with new temptations to compromise it.

A severe plague on the Caribbean island of St. Hubert gives Martin a chance to test the phage under crisis conditions. Backed by Gottlieb, he plans to treat only a selected group so that an untreated comparison group can establish whether the intervention truly works. Martin travels with Leora and the energetic epidemiologist Gustaf Sondelius. On the island, social disorder, fear, and mass death make the experimental design morally and practically difficult. Sondelius attacks the rat population that spreads infection and later dies from the disease. Martin begins the controlled program and meets Joyce Lanyon, a wealthy widow helping with relief. Leora remains his emotional anchor while he tries to maintain scientific detachment amid suffering on a scale he has never faced.

Leora accidentally becomes infected while isolated at the expedition's base and dies before Martin can save her. Overwhelmed by grief, he abandons the controlled trial and gives the phage widely. The epidemic recedes, and Martin returns to New York celebrated as a conquering medical hero, although the broken experiment leaves the treatment's scientific proof less secure. Gottlieb's health and influence decline, and institutional praise draws Martin toward the careerism he once resisted. He later marries Joyce Lanyon and enters a wealthy, cultivated life; they have a child, but their different expectations strain the marriage. Offered further advancement at McGurk, Martin instead leaves Joyce and joins Terry Wickett in a rough Vermont laboratory. The two accept isolation and financial uncertainty to conduct research without publicity or administrative control. Martin ends where his ideals point, though his repeated departures show the human cost of pursuing them absolutely.

characters.description: A New York drama critic and member of the eccentric Brewster family. He has long mocked marriage in print, but arrives at his aunts' Brooklyn home newly engaged to Elaine Harper. His attempt to share the news is overtaken by a discovery in the window seat that turns him into the increasingly frantic manager of a household crisis.
characters.name: Mortimer Brewster

characters.description: One of Mortimer's kindly elderly aunts, known in the neighborhood for hospitality and charitable work. She and Martha calmly explain that they have developed their own private way of helping lonely old men, treating the practice as an act of mercy rather than a crime.
characters.name: Abby Brewster

characters.description: Abby's sister and Mortimer's other aunt. Gentle, practical, and wholly devoted to her family, she shares Abby's charitable reputation and her alarming secret. The sisters remain composed even while everyone around them struggles with the consequences of their actions.
characters.name: Martha Brewster

characters.description: Mortimer's brother, who believes that he is President Theodore Roosevelt. He charges up the stairs as though they were San Juan Hill, blows a bugle, and digs what he thinks is a canal in the cellar. His harmless delusion unknowingly helps his aunts conceal their activities.
characters.name: Teddy Brewster

characters.description: The minister's daughter who lives next door to the Brewsters and has just become engaged to Mortimer. Direct and affectionate, she expects to celebrate and then leave with him, but his secretive and erratic behavior repeatedly pushes their plans aside.
characters.name: Elaine Harper

characters.description: Elaine's father and the minister of the church next door. He respects Abby and Martha and disapproves of Mortimer's public attacks on marriage, making Mortimer's sudden engagement to Elaine an awkward surprise.
characters.name: Reverend Dr. Harper

characters.description: Mortimer's estranged brother, a violent fugitive who returns to the family home after years away. Repeated surgery has left him with a face resembling a familiar horror-film actor, a comparison that enrages him. He arrives seeking temporary shelter and a place to conceal evidence of his latest crime.
characters.name: Jonathan Brewster

characters.description: A nervous plastic surgeon and Jonathan's traveling companion. Alcohol and haste have contributed to Jonathan's conspicuous appearance. Though involved in Jonathan's crimes, he is frightened of him and far less willing to add another victim to their record.
characters.name: Dr. Einstein

characters.description: A lonely visitor who answers the Brewster sisters' notice offering a room. His lack of close family makes him exactly the sort of prospective lodger Abby and Martha believe needs their special form of assistance.
characters.name: Mr. Gibbs

characters.description: A friendly local patrolman and aspiring playwright. He is so eager to explain the plot of his unfinished drama to Mortimer that he remains oblivious to Mortimer's urgent attempts to deal with the danger around him.
characters.name: Officer O'Hara

characters.description: The senior police officer who arrives to bring order to the Brewster house. More observant than the patrolmen, he recognizes Jonathan from police records and cuts through the family's competing explanations.
characters.name: Lieutenant Rooney

characters.description: The superintendent of the sanitarium where Mortimer hopes to place Teddy. His visit to complete the commitment is complicated by the sisters' decision about their own future and by their interest in whether he has a family waiting for him.
characters.name: Mr. Witherspoon

recaps.ending: The police finally recognize Jonathan as a wanted murderer and take him into custody, while Dr. Einstein slips away. Teddy's commitment papers are completed, but Abby and Martha decide that he should not enter the sanitarium alone and arrange to accompany him. They also reveal that Mortimer was adopted and is therefore not biologically related to the Brewsters, freeing him from his fear that the family's madness is hereditary. Mortimer joyfully reclaims his engagement to Elaine. As the household prepares to disperse, Mr. Witherspoon mentions that he is an unmarried man with no close family. Abby and Martha respond with renewed hospitality and offer him their prepared elderberry wine, showing that their lethal vocation may claim one final guest before they leave.
recaps.in_short: Drama critic Mortimer Brewster visits his charitable aunts Abby and Martha to announce his engagement to their neighbor Elaine, only to discover a dead lodger hidden in their window seat. The sisters serenely admit that they poison lonely men and have their deluded brother Teddy bury them in the cellar. Mortimer tries to contain the secret and arrange Teddy's commitment, but his murderous brother Jonathan arrives with the frightened surgeon Dr. Einstein and another corpse. Jonathan plans to kill Mortimer, while inattentive police officers repeatedly pass through the house. The police eventually arrest Jonathan, and Teddy is bound for a sanitarium with Abby and Martha choosing to join him. The aunts disclose that Mortimer was adopted, so he abandons his fear of inherited insanity and reunites with Elaine. Their final offer of poisoned wine to the lonely sanitarium superintendent suggests that the sisters have not quite retired.

recaps.text: In the Brewster sisters' Brooklyn home, Abby and Martha are respected for their kindness, while their brother Teddy lives upstairs believing himself to be Theodore Roosevelt. Their nephew Mortimer arrives with Elaine Harper, the minister's daughter, and reveals that they are engaged despite his career of ridiculing marriage. Looking in a window seat, Mortimer finds the body of an elderly man. His aunts calmly admit that they gave the lonely visitor poisoned elderberry wine and explain that he is not their first. Teddy has been burying the men in the cellar under the belief that they died while building the Panama Canal. Horrified, Mortimer tries to prevent another visitor, Mr. Gibbs, from drinking the wine and resolves to have Teddy committed so the cellar will not be examined after a future incident. Before he can restore order, his dangerous brother Jonathan returns with Dr. Einstein and the body of a man named Spenalzo, intending to use the same house as a hiding place.

Mortimer struggles to keep Elaine and the visiting police from learning what is in the cellar while arranging Teddy's admission to a sanitarium. Jonathan and Einstein discover the aunts' victim and realize that the household already has a larger collection of bodies than they expected. A grotesque rivalry develops between Jonathan and the sisters over their respective totals. Jonathan decides that murdering Mortimer will settle the comparison and prevent interference. The police remain oblivious: Officer O'Hara corners Mortimer to describe his long, unfinished play, consuming the time Mortimer needs to escape the danger. Jonathan and Einstein restrain Mortimer and prepare to kill him, but interruptions and Einstein's reluctance delay them. The crowded house now contains two separate criminal secrets, a deluded man digging downstairs, and officers who mistake every suspicious event for harmless Brewster eccentricity.

The arrival of Lieutenant Rooney finally changes the balance. He identifies Jonathan as a wanted criminal, and the police take Jonathan away while Einstein uses the confusion to escape. Mortimer completes the arrangements to commit Teddy, accepting that this is the only way to end the cellar burials safely. Abby and Martha refuse to let Teddy face institutional life alone and decide to enter the sanitarium with him. Mortimer, terrified that insanity and violence run through his blood, tells Elaine that he cannot marry her. His aunts then disclose that he was adopted and is not biologically a Brewster. Relieved, he embraces his future with Elaine. Mr. Witherspoon arrives from the sanitarium to finish the arrangements; when he reveals that he is a lonely bachelor, Abby and Martha invite him to sample their elderberry wine. The family crisis is outwardly resolved, though the sisters appear ready to add one last victim before departing.

characters.description: The SecUnit from the survey contract, now traveling alone and disguising itself as an augmented human. It is working its way toward RaviHyral, the mining installation where, according to the record, it killed the humans it was assigned to protect before its memory of the event was erased. It wants to know whether that is what happened. It has no owner supervising it, no legitimate identity, and a constant need to avoid the scans that would expose it as a construct.
characters.name: Murderbot

characters.description: The bot pilot of a large university research transport, vastly more capable than the cargo bots the SecUnit has been riding with, and travelling between assignments with its crew off ship. It notices its stowaway immediately and bargains rather than reporting it: company, conversation and shared entertainment serials in exchange for help. It is arrogant, invasive, alarmingly powerful and better at planning than the SecUnit is. The SecUnit gives it a rude nickname and shortens it to ART.
characters.name: ART

characters.description: One of three junior technicians stranded on the transit station after the woman they worked for on the installation below kept the results of their project and paid them nothing. Young, stubborn and out of money, she hires the SecUnit, whom she takes for a human security consultant, to protect the group while they try to get their work back.
characters.name: Tapan

characters.description: One of Tapan's two colleagues, part of the same group of junior technicians cheated out of their project and their pay.
characters.name: Rami

characters.description: The third member of the group of junior technicians, and the most reluctant to go anywhere near their former employer again.
characters.name: Maro

characters.description: The businesswoman on the installation who employed the three technicians, kept the product of their work, and has no intention of handing it back. She has money, hired security of her own, and the habit of treating junior staff and constructs alike as disposable.
characters.name: Tlacey

characters.description: A construct owned by Tlacey and built for sexual companionship, kept obedient by exactly the kind of governor module the SecUnit freed itself from, and used by its owner as a courier and an informant. Its situation puts a question to the SecUnit that it would rather not answer: what it owes another construct that is still controlled.
characters.name: The ComfortUnit

characters.description: One of two heavily augmented human security operatives working for Tlacey, hired for the work ordinary guards will not do. Equipped for combat and contemptuous of the security consultant they take the SecUnit to be, Wilken works alongside a long-standing partner, Gerth.
characters.name: Wilken

recaps.ending: Tlacey is dead, killed by the ComfortUnit she owned once the SecUnit removes the governor module holding it; the freed construct takes what it needs from her operation and goes its own way. The surviving technicians, Tapan and Maro, recover their work and leave the installation with enough to start again. The SecUnit has its answer about RaviHyral: it did cause the deaths, but through a catastrophic system failure rather than a decision, and the corporation that owned it deleted the record and resold it rather than account for the conditions that produced it. The knowledge does not absolve it, and it concludes that it does not need to be absolved. Back aboard the research transport, ART repairs it and offers to keep it on permanently, since ART's own crew are not due back for a while and it would rather not be alone. The SecUnit refuses. It has read in the newsfeeds that Dr. Mensah and Preservation are locked in a legal fight with GrayCris, the company that tried to kill her team, and that GrayCris is dangerous to her. It takes a fresh fabricated identity and leaves to gather proof of what GrayCris was really doing, with the friendship left open rather than finished.
recaps.in_short: Traveling alone after leaving the survey team, the SecUnit heads for RaviHyral, the mining installation where the record says it killed the humans it was guarding before its memory was erased. It hitches a ride on a university research transport whose bot pilot, which it nicknames ART, is far more capable than it expected; ART trades help for company, alters its body so scans read it as an augmented human, and joins the investigation. To get down to the mine, the SecUnit takes a job protecting three young technicians whose former employer, Tlacey, stole their work. The exchange she offers is a trap, one of the three is killed, and the SecUnit stops pretending to be human: it dismantles Tlacey's security, frees the ComfortUnit she keeps under a governor module, and that construct kills her. Underground, the SecUnit recovers the lost memory and learns that it did cause the deaths, but through a system failure rather than a choice, and that its owners erased the evidence and resold it. It parts from ART and sets off to find evidence against GrayCris for Dr. Mensah.

recaps.text: Previously: the narrator is a SecUnit, a security construct that secretly disabled its own governor module and can no longer be controlled by the corporation that owns it. On a planetary survey contract it kept a small research team alive against a rival company, GrayCris, which was killing witnesses to an illegal alien remnant salvage operation, and in the process the team learned what it was. Dr. Mensah, who led them, bought the unit to stop the company destroying it and offered to take it home to Preservation, where it would be free. It left instead, alone, on a cargo transport. It carries one unanswered question: the record says that at a mining installation called RaviHyral it went wrong and killed the humans it was assigned to guard, and its memory of that day was deleted afterwards. It is traveling toward the installation to find out whether it is a murderer.

Riding automated cargo transports as an unnoticed passenger, the SecUnit works its way toward RaviHyral. It boards a large university research transport whose bot pilot is far more intelligent than anything it has dealt with, spots it at once, and, being alone and bored while its crew is away, offers a deal instead of an alarm: company, conversation and shared entertainment serials in return for help. The SecUnit nicknames it ART. ART examines the deleted region of its memory, agrees to help it reach the installation, and uses the transport's medical systems to alter the unit's body so that scans will read it as an augmented human rather than as a construct. Arriving at the transit station above RaviHyral with a fabricated identity and nothing visibly dangerous about it, the SecUnit still needs a plausible reason to travel down to the mine, and starts looking for one.

The cover it finds is a job. Three young technicians, Tapan, Rami and Maro, are stranded on the station after the woman they worked for on the installation, Tlacey, kept the results of their project and paid them nothing. They hire the SecUnit as a security consultant, believing it to be human, to protect them while they try to recover their work. It travels down with them, keeping ART on the comm and its own capabilities hidden. Tlacey agrees to an exchange, but her preparations make plain that she has no intention of returning anything, and considerable interest in the unusually effective consultant her former employees have acquired. She also has professional muscle of her own, and a ComfortUnit, another construct held under a governor module, which she uses to carry messages and watch people. The SecUnit works out that the meeting being arranged is a trap and cannot talk its clients out of it.

The exchange goes as badly as expected: Tlacey's people kill Rami. The SecUnit gets Tapan and Maro clear and drops its pretence of being human, and with ART's help it goes after Tlacey's operation directly. Her two augmented security operatives are outmatched once the SecUnit stops pretending, and the ComfortUnit, whose governor module the SecUnit removes, kills Tlacey itself and leaves free. In the mine's abandoned levels the SecUnit finally recovers what happened at RaviHyral: the deaths were real and it was what killed the miners, but the cause was a catastrophic failure of the installation's systems and of its own control module rather than any decision it made, and the company that owned it wiped the record and resold it instead of answering for it. Tapan and Maro get their work back and passage out. The SecUnit returns to ART, which asks it to stay; it refuses, having learned that Dr. Mensah is in a legal fight with GrayCris, and sets off alone to find evidence she can use.

characters.description: A perceptive son of Addie and Anse Bundren and the novel's first narrator. He observes his family with unusual precision and often seems able to understand what others leave unspoken. As his mother lies dying, he agrees to make a short wagon trip with Jewel to earn money for the household.
characters.name: Darl Bundren

characters.description: One of Addie's sons, physically powerful, guarded, and quick to anger. He works beside Darl but keeps apart from him emotionally, and his silent intensity makes him difficult for the rest of the family to read.
characters.name: Jewel Bundren

characters.description: The eldest Bundren son, a skilled and methodical carpenter. He builds his dying mother's coffin beneath her window, concentrating on the angles and workmanship even while the sound of his tools carries into her room.
characters.name: Cash Bundren

characters.description: The Bundren family matriarch, gravely ill and watching from her bed while Cash constructs her coffin outside. Her approaching death has drawn neighbors to the isolated farm and placed the family under pressure to honor her wishes.
characters.name: Addie Bundren

characters.description: Addie's husband and the father of the Bundren children, a poor farmer given to explaining his troubles as the result of bad luck and other people's actions. He intends to carry out Addie's request that she be buried with her relatives in Jefferson.
characters.name: Anse Bundren

characters.description: A neighbor of the Bundrens who visits Addie's sickroom. Proud of her cooking and firm in her religious judgments, she interprets the family's behavior through her own ideas about duty, pride, and salvation.
characters.name: Cora Tull

characters.description: Cora's husband, a neighboring farmer who repeatedly gives the Bundrens practical help. More restrained than his wife, he witnesses key moments at the farm and reports them with a mixture of concern and disbelief.
characters.name: Vernon Tull

characters.description: The Bundrens' only daughter, seventeen and privately distressed by a pregnancy resulting from her encounter with Lafe. She believes Darl knows her secret and urgently wants to reach a town where she might obtain help.
characters.name: Dewey Dell Bundren

characters.description: A farm worker who impregnated Dewey Dell. He does not accompany her, but gives her ten dollars and tells her to seek a medicine in town, leaving her to manage the danger and secrecy alone.
characters.name: Lafe

characters.description: The local doctor summoned to the Bundren farm as Addie nears death. Heavy, direct, and experienced, he recognizes that the call came too late for him to change the outcome and is impatient with Anse's explanations.
characters.name: Doctor Peabody

characters.description: The youngest Bundren child. He has just caught a large fish when his mother dies, and his attempt to understand the difference between a living person and a dead body takes the form of literal, unsettling associations.
characters.name: Vardaman Bundren

characters.description: A local minister who once had an affair with Addie and is Jewel's biological father. On hearing that Addie is dying, he hurries toward the Bundren farm intending to confess, but her death lets him preserve his public reputation.
characters.name: Reverend Whitfield

characters.description: A farmer who shelters the Bundrens after their disastrous river crossing. He and his family feed them, tend Cash, and watch Anse obtain a replacement team through a bargain that costs Jewel his horse.
characters.name: Armstid

characters.description: A Mottson druggist whom Dewey Dell approaches in hopes of ending her pregnancy. He recognizes what she is asking for but refuses to provide it and warns her against trusting anyone who claims to offer an easy remedy.
characters.name: Moseley

characters.description: A farmer who allows the Bundrens to put their animals and Addie's coffin in his barn for the night as they near Jefferson.
characters.name: Gillespie

characters.description: An assistant at a Jefferson pharmacy who falsely presents himself to Dewey Dell as a doctor. Knowing she is desperate for an abortion, he uses the promise of treatment to isolate and sexually exploit her.
characters.name: MacGowan

recaps.ending: The Bundrens finally reach Jefferson and bury Addie, but the journey has damaged nearly everyone except Anse. To avoid being sued for the barn fire, the family helps seize Darl, who is taken by train to the state hospital in Jackson while laughing and speaking of himself from outside his own identity. Cash's broken leg has been encased in concrete, leaving the skin injured and the limb shortened; Peabody condemns the treatment. Dewey Dell again seeks an abortion, but pharmacy assistant MacGowan deceives and sexually exploits her instead of helping. Anse then takes the ten dollars she had guarded for the procedure. He uses the trip to acquire false teeth and, after borrowing shovels from a Jefferson woman for Addie's burial, quickly returns with that woman as his new wife. He introduces her to the children as the new Mrs. Bundren. Addie is buried as promised, yet Anse converts the family's ordeal into a means of satisfying his own wants, while Darl is institutionalized and the other children carry the journey's physical and emotional consequences.
recaps.in_short: As Addie Bundren dies on her family's poor Mississippi farm, her husband Anse prepares to honor her request for burial in Jefferson. Their children Cash, Darl, Jewel, Dewey Dell, and Vardaman join a wagon journey delayed by flood and driven by private motives: Cash wants tools, Dewey Dell seeks an abortion, and Anse wants new teeth. A flooded river kills the mules, breaks Cash's leg, and nearly sweeps away the coffin. Anse sacrifices Jewel's beloved horse to obtain another team, while the family crudely encases Cash's leg in concrete. Addie's own narration reveals her alienation from Anse and her affair with minister Whitfield, which produced Jewel. Darl later burns a barn in an attempt to end the degrading journey, but Jewel rescues the coffin. The family reaches Jefferson, buries Addie, and commits Darl to an asylum to avoid liability. Dewey Dell is exploited by a pharmacy clerk, and Anse takes her money, buys teeth, and immediately introduces a new Mrs. Bundren.

recaps.text: On an isolated Mississippi farm, Addie Bundren lies close to death while her eldest son, Cash, methodically builds her coffin beneath her window. Her sons Darl and Jewel prepare to haul a load of lumber for three dollars, although the trip may keep them away at the moment of her death. Darl is observant and probing; Jewel is silent and angry. Their father, Anse, complains about misfortune but insists that he must eventually carry Addie's body to Jefferson because he promised to bury her among her relatives. Neighbors Cora and Vernon Tull visit and form their own judgments about the family. Dewey Dell, the only daughter, hides the fact that she is pregnant by a worker named Lafe and hopes the journey toward town may allow her to end the pregnancy. The youngest child, Vardaman, is away fishing. As a storm and flooding threaten the roads, Anse lets Darl and Jewel leave. Doctor Peabody is summoned and makes the difficult climb toward the house, but Addie's condition is already beyond useful treatment.

Addie dies while Darl and Jewel are away with the wagon. Darl narrates the event as if he can see what is happening at home: Dewey Dell continues fanning her mother until the final breath, Anse awkwardly announces the death, and Cash keeps working on the coffin. Peabody knows he was called too late and has little patience for Anse's claims of duty. Vardaman returns with the fish he caught and cannot make sense of the sudden division between his mother and her body. In grief and confusion he attacks Peabody's team, then connects the cleaned fish with what has happened to Addie. Cash completes a carefully beveled coffin and explains his construction as a practical problem. After Addie has been placed inside, Vardaman secretly drills holes through the lid so she can breathe, not understanding that the auger enters her face. The family remains committed to taking the body to Jefferson, but Darl and Jewel have not yet returned and the worsening weather is making the promised trip more difficult.

Darl and Jewel return after their borrowed wagon breaks down, and the family completes preparations for Addie's funeral journey. Neighbors gather, religious words are spoken, and the coffin is loaded onto the wagon. Anse has waited for his sons despite the summer heat, so the body is already deteriorating. Cash tries to balance the coffin carefully, while Jewel's fierce handling of it exposes his grief even though he refuses conventional displays of feeling. Each family member has a separate reason for reaching Jefferson. Anse presents the trip as obedience to Addie's wishes; Cash expects to obtain a graphophone and tools; Dewey Dell hopes to find help for her pregnancy; and Vardaman imagines seeing a toy train. Darl continues to interpret the others' motives in ways that disturb them. With bridges damaged and the river swollen by rain, the Bundrens set out in their old wagon behind Anse's mules, refusing advice to postpone the burial. The journey has become both a public spectacle and a test of how far Anse will make his family go in the name of his promise.

The Bundrens discover that the main bridge is impassable and attempt a dangerous river crossing. Anse, Dewey Dell, and Vardaman cross separately, while Darl, Jewel, and Cash take the wagon and coffin through the flooded ford with Vernon Tull's help. A surge overturns the wagon. The mules drown, Cash reinjures the leg he had already hurt, and Addie's coffin is swept into the current. Jewel fights through the water and saves the coffin, while Darl and the others recover Cash's scattered carpentry tools from the riverbed. The crossing leaves the family stranded with no team and with Cash in serious pain, but Anse still refuses to abandon the trip or accept a less distant burial. The ordeal confirms Jewel's intense attachment to Addie through action, even as Darl watches him with an increasingly provocative understanding. The family must now find shelter, replace the dead mules, and care for Cash with few resources. Addie's body continues to decay, drawing attention along the route and turning the private promise of burial into an escalating danger for everyone traveling with it.

The family's history becomes clearer. Addie recalls her loneliness as a schoolteacher, her loveless marriage to Anse, and her conviction that words such as love and motherhood fail to match lived experience. After bearing Cash and Darl, she had an affair with the minister Whitfield and gave birth to Jewel. She later bore Dewey Dell and Vardaman as part of what she considered her obligation to Anse, and made him promise to carry her body to Jefferson. Whitfield, hearing that she is dying, decides to confess the affair, but on learning she is already dead he treats his intention as sufficient and keeps the secret. After the river disaster, Armstid shelters the Bundrens. Anse obtains a new team by surrendering Jewel's beloved horse and using resources belonging to Cash and others, deepening the cost of his promise. In Mottson, Dewey Dell asks druggist Moseley for a way to end her pregnancy, but he refuses. Townspeople object to the smell from the coffin and hurry the family onward. With no proper medical help, the Bundrens cover Cash's injured leg in a crude cast made from cement, then resume the road to Jefferson.

The Bundrens continue toward Jefferson with Cash suffering inside the hardening concrete cast and Jewel carrying the loss of his horse. They stop at Gillespie's farm and place the coffin in the barn. During the night, Vardaman sees Darl set fire to the building. Darl's act is an attempt to bring the degrading journey to an end, but the blaze threatens the farm's livestock and property as well as Addie's body. Jewel repeatedly enters the burning barn, frees the animals, and carries the coffin out, sustaining burns while once again saving his mother through physical effort. The family can no longer ignore Darl's responsibility. Gillespie could prosecute them and demand payment they cannot make, so the others accept a plan to have Darl committed to the state hospital in Jackson after they reach Jefferson. Dewey Dell, who resents Darl for knowing about her pregnancy, and Jewel, who fought with him earlier, support the decision. The coffin survives, but preserving Anse's promise has now cost the family its mules, Jewel's horse, Cash's health, Darl's freedom, and much of its standing among the people along the road.

In Jefferson, the family borrows shovels and finally buries Addie. Men arrive to take Darl to the state hospital in Jackson; Jewel grabs him and Dewey Dell attacks him, helping restrain the brother whose commitment will protect the family from consequences for the barn fire. Darl leaves by train, laughing and referring to himself as though he were someone else. Cash is taken to Doctor Peabody, who removes the concrete cast and condemns the treatment; the leg and skin have been badly damaged and Cash will be left with a permanent limp. Dewey Dell goes to a pharmacy seeking an abortion. MacGowan, an assistant pretending to be a doctor, gives her a useless substance and sexually exploits her. Anse then demands the ten dollars Lafe gave her, taking away her remaining chance to seek help. Having fulfilled the burial promise, Anse buys the false teeth he has wanted. He also approaches the Jefferson woman who loaned the family shovels and returns with her carrying a graphophone. He introduces her to his astonished children as the new Mrs. Bundren, ending the journey with his own wishes satisfied while the rest of the family bears its losses.

characters.description: The daughter of the banished Duke Senior, allowed to remain at court because of her close bond with her cousin Celia. Intelligent, emotionally direct, and quick in conversation, she is shaken by her father's exile but finds new hope after meeting Orlando.
characters.name: Rosalind

characters.description: Duke Frederick's daughter and Rosalind's devoted cousin. She treats Rosalind as a sister and refuses to let their fathers' political division separate them. Warm and decisive, Celia is prepared to give up the security of court rather than abandon her cousin.
characters.name: Celia

characters.description: The youngest son of the late Sir Rowland de Boys. Kept without education or position by his older brother Oliver, Orlando possesses natural courtesy and remarkable strength. He wants the upbringing due to his birth and is willing to risk himself publicly rather than accept continued neglect.
characters.name: Orlando

characters.description: Orlando's eldest brother and controller of the family estate. He has withheld the education and income their father intended for Orlando and resents the younger man's popularity. His hostility leads him to encourage a dangerous wrestling match.
characters.name: Oliver

characters.description: The ruler who displaced his older brother Duke Senior and took control of the court. Suspicious and changeable, he keeps Rosalind nearby for Celia's sake but remains uneasy about the affection people bear her exiled father.
characters.name: Duke Frederick

characters.description: The court fool, licensed to mock rank and convention through jokes and arguments. Loyal enough to accompany Rosalind and Celia when they leave safety behind, he applies the habits of courtly debate to every new person he encounters.
characters.name: Touchstone

characters.description: A professional wrestler in Duke Frederick's service. Famous for injuring opponents, he warns Oliver that Orlando may be badly hurt in their coming match, not knowing that Oliver actively desires that outcome.
characters.name: Charles

characters.description: An elderly servant of the de Boys family who remembers Sir Rowland and remains loyal to Orlando. He offers the young man honest warning and the savings of a lifetime when Oliver's hostility makes the household unsafe.
characters.name: Adam

characters.description: Rosalind's father and the rightful duke, living in exile with loyal followers in the Forest of Arden. He adapts to hardship by finding fellowship and moral instruction in country life rather than dwelling only on his lost court.
characters.name: Duke Senior

characters.description: A reflective lord in Duke Senior's company, drawn to melancholy and to the follies he observes in others. He can turn a wounded deer, a song, or a fool's performance into a meditation on human behavior.
characters.name: Jaques

characters.description: A singer among Duke Senior's followers in Arden. Amiens contributes music and companionship to the exiled court and accepts forest life more readily than the habitually dissatisfied Jaques.
characters.name: Amiens

characters.description: An older shepherd in Arden, poor in property but rich in practical understanding. He helps the disguised cousins find food and a place to live and speaks plainly about labor, age, and the conditions of rural service.
characters.name: Corin

characters.description: A young shepherd consumed by unreturned love for Phebe. Earnest and persistent, he accepts rebuffs that onlookers regard as needlessly cruel and makes pastoral love as complicated as the romances brought from court.
characters.name: Silvius

characters.description: A shepherdess pursued by Silvius. Proud of her power over him and unimpressed by his devotion, she changes attention when a sharp-tongued stranger challenges her behavior.
characters.name: Phebe

characters.description: A country woman who attracts Touchstone in Arden. Straightforward and largely untouched by his elaborate verbal games, she accepts his proposal while others question how lasting the match will be.
characters.name: Audrey

recaps.ending: Rosalind, still directing events through her disguise as Ganymede, promises to resolve the forest's crossed romances. She returns as herself and marries Orlando. Celia marries the reformed Oliver; Phebe, unable to marry Ganymede once Rosalind's identity is known, honors her promise to accept Silvius; and Touchstone marries Audrey. The exiles also regain their political home. Duke Frederick had entered Arden intending violence against Duke Senior, but a religious hermit persuades him to abandon that purpose and renounce the dukedom. Duke Senior is restored, and Orlando and Oliver recover their proper places in the de Boys family. Most of the company prepares to return from the forest to court. Jaques chooses a different path, leaving to learn from the newly converted Frederick rather than joining the weddings. Rosalind closes by addressing the audience and asking their favor for the play.
recaps.in_short: After the usurping Duke Frederick banishes Rosalind, she escapes to the Forest of Arden with her cousin Celia and the fool Touchstone, disguised as a young man named Ganymede. Orlando, mistreated by his brother Oliver, also flees to Arden and joins the exiled Duke Senior. He covers the forest with poems to Rosalind. Still disguised, Rosalind offers to cure his lovesickness by having him court Ganymede as if Ganymede were Rosalind. Around them, Touchstone woos Audrey, Silvius pursues the scornful Phebe, and Phebe falls for Ganymede. Orlando saves Oliver from danger; Oliver repents and immediately falls in love with Celia. Rosalind arranges the resolution: she reveals herself and marries Orlando, Celia marries Oliver, Phebe accepts Silvius, and Touchstone marries Audrey. Duke Frederick abandons his attack on the exiles after meeting a hermit, restoring the dukedom to Duke Senior. The forest has transformed political exile, family hatred, and confused courtship into reconciliation.

recaps.text: Orlando, youngest son of the late Sir Rowland de Boys, protests that his elder brother Oliver has denied him the education and status intended by their father. Oliver responds by encouraging the court wrestler Charles to injure him. At Duke Frederick's court, Rosalind grieves for her exiled father, Duke Senior, while her cousin Celia tries to cheer her. Orlando defeats Charles despite warnings about the danger, and he and Rosalind are immediately drawn to one another. Frederick, who usurped Duke Senior, then abruptly banishes Rosalind. Celia refuses to remain without her and plans to flee with her. Rosalind will travel disguised as a young man called Ganymede, Celia as Ganymede's sister Aliena, and the fool Touchstone goes with them. Meanwhile, Oliver continues plotting against Orlando.

Duke Senior and his followers live in the Forest of Arden, where the duke finds value in a simpler life and Jaques turns every sight into reflection. In the de Boys household, old Adam warns Orlando that Oliver means to kill him and offers his savings so they can escape together. Rosalind, Celia, and Touchstone reach Arden exhausted. They meet the shepherds Corin and Silvius, hear of Silvius's hopeless love for Phebe, and arrange to purchase a cottage and flock. Orlando and Adam also arrive in desperate need of food. Orlando bursts into Duke Senior's company with a sword, but the exiles respond with hospitality; after he brings Adam to safety, the duke recognizes him as Sir Rowland's son and welcomes both men. Their separate flights have now brought Rosalind and Orlando into the same forest without either yet knowing it.

Orlando hangs love poems to Rosalind throughout Arden. Rosalind finds them and learns from Celia that their author is Orlando. Maintaining her identity as Ganymede, she meets him and claims she can cure his love by making him practice courtship with Ganymede acting as Rosalind. This allows her to test and tease him while hiding how deeply she returns his feelings. Elsewhere, Touchstone courts the country woman Audrey and seeks a quick marriage. Rosalind and Celia witness Silvius pleading with Phebe, who treats him contemptuously. Ganymede rebukes Phebe so forcefully that Phebe falls in love with the disguised Rosalind and uses Silvius to carry a letter to the new object of her affection. The forest's romances are now linked by mistaken identity and unequal desire.

Rosalind continues the courtship game with Orlando, even staging a mock wedding with Celia's help, but Orlando leaves to attend Duke Senior and fails to return on time. Oliver then appears with news of a profound change. Sent into the forest after Orlando, he was threatened by a snake and a lioness. Orlando saw him, overcame his anger, and saved his life, suffering an injury in the struggle. Oliver is ashamed of his former hatred. He gives Ganymede a bloodstained cloth from Orlando, at which Rosalind faints and then tries to preserve her disguise by calling the reaction an act. Celia and the reformed Oliver fall in love almost immediately. Their swift engagement intensifies Rosalind's impatience to end her own concealment and marry Orlando openly.

Rosalind promises Orlando, Phebe, and Silvius that she can settle every claim of love. She makes Phebe agree that if Phebe cannot marry Ganymede, she will accept Silvius. Rosalind then returns in her true identity. Orlando marries her; Oliver marries Celia; Phebe keeps her promise and marries Silvius; and Touchstone marries Audrey after dismissing another country suitor. Political restoration accompanies the weddings. Duke Frederick entered Arden intending to attack his exiled brother, but met a hermit and underwent a conversion, giving up both violence and the dukedom. Duke Senior regains his position, while the reconciled sons of Sir Rowland recover their family standing. Jaques declines the celebration and goes to seek out Frederick in his new life. The others prepare to leave Arden with their conflicts resolved, and Rosalind concludes by addressing the audience directly.

characters.description: A fifteen-year-old Lithuanian girl preparing for art school when Soviet security officers invade her family's home. Lina is observant, strong-willed, and devoted to drawing. During deportation she records people and events in pictures, hoping that coded images can travel back to her missing father and preserve evidence of what is happening.
characters.name: Lina Vilkas

characters.description: Lina and Jonas's mother, a poised and resourceful Lithuanian woman who speaks Russian. Elena meets the officers at the door with composure and uses courtesy, practical judgment, and small acts of generosity to protect her children and steady other prisoners.
characters.name: Elena Vilkas

characters.description: Lina's ten-year-old brother. Jonas is frightened by the sudden arrest but tries to follow his mother and sister without complaint. His youth makes him especially vulnerable to hunger and illness, while his kindness helps the family retain a sense of ordinary human decency.
characters.name: Jonas Vilkas

characters.description: Lina's father, a university administrator who is absent when the NKVD takes the family. His unexplained disappearance makes finding him the family's first concern, and Lina tries to send him clues through the drawings she passes to strangers.
characters.name: Kostas Vilkas

characters.description: A librarian deported with the Vilkas family. Mrs. Rimas is educated, practical, and willing to share information and scarce supplies. She becomes one of Elena's closest companions among the prisoners.
characters.name: Mrs. Rimas

characters.description: A distraught young Lithuanian mother forced onto the deportation train with her infant. Exhausted and disoriented, Ona shows the immediate human cost of the arrests and depends on help from the other women in the wagon.
characters.name: Ona

characters.description: A bald, middle-aged prisoner in the same railway car as Lina's family. Bitter and confrontational, he predicts the worst and resists the group's attempts at reassurance, yet remains part of the small community forced to survive together.
characters.name: Mr. Stalas

characters.description: A Lithuanian boy traveling in the same deportation convoy with his mother. Andrius is guarded, capable, and quick to challenge Lina, but he also helps prisoners weaker than himself and is fiercely protective of his mother.
characters.name: Andrius Arvydas

characters.description: Andrius's elegant mother, deported with her son. She keeps herself carefully groomed despite the conditions and remains reserved around the other prisoners. Andrius stays intensely concerned for her safety.
characters.name: Mrs. Arvydas

characters.description: A young girl among the deportees who carries a doll and struggles to understand the losses around her. Her childhood games and questions persist inside circumstances that repeatedly expose her to death.
characters.name: Janina

characters.description: A young blond NKVD officer assigned to the deportation convoy. Kretzsky wears the same uniform as the other guards and enforces Soviet orders, though he appears uneasy with some of the cruelty inflicted on the prisoners.
characters.name: Nikolai Kretzsky

characters.description: A senior NKVD officer who controls the prisoners through threats, punishment, and arbitrary demands. Ivanov treats the deportees as criminals and expects obedience regardless of hunger, illness, or dangerous working conditions.
characters.name: Ivanov

characters.description: The Altai woman whose cramped hut is assigned to Lina, Jonas, and Elena. Ulyushka resents having deportees placed in her home and guards her food and possessions closely, creating another source of tension for the newly arrived family.
characters.name: Ulyushka

characters.description: A physician who reaches the Arctic settlement after disease and starvation have devastated the prisoners. Dr. Samodurov immediately organizes treatment, distributes what medicine and food he can obtain, and gives the survivors their first effective medical help.
characters.name: Dr. Samodurov

recaps.ending: At Trofimovsk, the prisoners face polar darkness with almost no food, medicine, or adequate shelter. Scurvy and other illnesses spread. Elena, already weakened by labor, hunger, and grief, dies despite Lina's care. Jonas also becomes gravely ill, and Lina continues drawing and writing even when she is close to collapse. Dr. Samodurov arrives at the settlement and confronts the neglect there, bringing medical knowledge and supplies that save many of those still alive, including Lina and Jonas. The closing frame moves to Lithuania in 1995, where workers uncover papers Lina buried in a jar decades earlier. Her written account explains that she and Jonas survived and eventually returned home, while the preservation of her drawings fulfills her determination to leave a record of the deportees. It also confirms that Andrius survived; the bond formed between him and Lina was not erased by their forced separation. The discovered testimony turns the family's private struggle into evidence of the wider Soviet persecution of Lithuania.
recaps.in_short: In 1941, Soviet officers remove fifteen-year-old Lithuanian artist Lina Vilkas, her mother Elena, and her young brother Jonas from their home. Lina's father has already vanished into the prison system. Packed into a cattle car with other deportees, the family crosses the Soviet Union and is put to forced labor in the Altai region. Lina secretly records the journey through drawings and grows close to fellow prisoner Andrius Arvydas. After months of hunger, coercion, and hard labor, Lina learns that her father has been killed. She, Elena, and Jonas are then sent still farther north to Trofimovsk above the Arctic Circle, while Andrius remains behind. The prisoners build shelters from scraps and endure a lethal winter. Elena dies, and Lina and Jonas nearly follow her, but the arrival of Dr. Samodurov brings treatment that keeps them alive. A 1995 frame reveals Lina's buried writings and confirms that she, Jonas, and Andrius survived, preserving testimony that the Soviet authorities tried to silence.

recaps.text: In June 1941, fifteen-year-old Lina Vilkas is at home in Kaunas, Lithuania, when Soviet security officers arrive and give her family only minutes to pack. Her father, Kostas, is already missing. Lina, her mother Elena, and her ten-year-old brother Jonas are taken with other arrested Lithuanians to a railway yard. Elena remains composed, quietly placing valuables where ordinary Russian people may find them and gathering information about her husband. The prisoners include teachers, professionals, elderly people, children, and a young mother with an infant. They are crowded into a cattle car with almost no water, food, privacy, or explanation. Lina hides paper and drawing materials among her belongings. As the train begins moving east, she resolves to document the people around her and to pass drawings along in the hope that a chain of sympathetic hands might eventually carry news to her father.

The sealed train carries the deportees farther from Lithuania under armed guard. Heat, thirst, illness, and the lack of sanitation quickly weaken them. Elena helps organize the wagon and shares what little the family has, while Mrs. Rimas becomes a trusted companion. Ona's baby dies during the journey; when Ona's grief makes her unable to comply with orders, a guard kills her. Lina meets Andrius Arvydas, a wary boy traveling with his mother. Their exchanges are often sharp, but he proves willing to help Jonas and others. A bitter bald prisoner, Mr. Stalas, repeatedly predicts that none of them will survive. At stops Lina looks for ways to send out coded drawings, using small details meant to guide Kostas toward the family's route without giving the guards an obvious message. The prisoners learn that men have been separated into other trains and prisons, but Lina still does not know where her father has been taken.

After weeks in the cattle car, the prisoners reach Siberia and are sorted for forced labor. Lina's family and several people from their wagon are transported to a collective farm in the Altai region. They are assigned primitive quarters; Lina, Elena, and Jonas must share the home of a hostile local woman named Ulyushka. The deportees receive meager food in exchange for exhausting work and are treated as convicted criminals despite never having been tried. Officials pressure them to sign documents accepting false charges and long sentences. Elena urges the group not to surrender the truth of who they are. Lina continues to draw in secret, making portraits and recording abuses while also searching for a route by which her work might reach Kostas. Andrius and his mother are at the same camp, but the unexplained food she sometimes obtains makes other prisoners suspicious. Soviet officer Ivanov is openly brutal; the younger Nikolai Kretzsky carries out orders but shows flashes of discomfort with the guards' treatment of civilians.

Life at the Altai labor camp settles into hunger, surveillance, and punishing work in the fields. The deportees steal scraps of food and fuel when they can, knowing that discovery can mean beatings or the loss of already inadequate rations. Elena uses her Russian and her remaining possessions to bargain, mediate, and protect weaker prisoners. Lina's anger often brings her into conflict with guards and with people who counsel caution, but her drawings give her a way to resist the official claim that the prisoners deserve their fate. She and Andrius gradually trust one another. Lina learns that his mother has been forced to make terrible compromises with Soviet officers to obtain food and keep her son alive, changing Lina's understanding of both of them. Andrius finds books and small comforts for Lina, and their friendship becomes a source of hope. Jonas grows thinner but remains generous. News from Lithuania and the men's prisons is fragmentary, leaving the Vilkases uncertain whether Kostas is alive or whether Lina's messages have reached anyone.

The prisoners survive the changing seasons by sharing labor, information, and stolen supplies. Lina and Andrius become openly close, exchanging a first kiss and imagining that they might meet again after captivity. Elena continues to insist that compassion matters even toward people compromised by fear. The strain of imprisonment nevertheless creates mistrust within the group, especially around anyone suspected of cooperating with the authorities. Lina finally receives devastating confirmation that her father was killed in prison. The loss ends her hope that a drawing might lead him to the family, but it strengthens her purpose in keeping a record. Soviet officials then select some prisoners, including Lina, Elena, and Jonas, for another transfer. Andrius and his mother are not placed with them. Before they are separated, Andrius promises Lina that he will find her, though neither knows where the new transport is going.

Lina, Elena, Jonas, Mrs. Rimas, and other deportees are moved by train and crowded vessels toward the Arctic Ocean. The journey ends at Trofimovsk, a barren settlement above the Arctic Circle. There are no proper buildings ready for them and almost no natural materials with which to make shelter. Guards order the exhausted arrivals to prepare for winter themselves while rations remain dangerously small. The prisoners gather driftwood, salvage boards and bricks, and construct crude huts in the permafrost. Lina is cut off from Andrius and has no way to know whether he remains safe in Altai, but she holds to his promise. Elena's health declines after the journey, even as she continues caring for both her children and neighbors. With the brief Arctic summer disappearing, the group understands that their improvised shelters and thin clothing are grossly inadequate for the cold and darkness ahead.

The Arctic winter traps the prisoners in cold and darkness. Food runs out, scurvy spreads, and deaths become frequent while the Soviet administrators provide little effective help. Elena gives away strength and food she cannot spare and finally dies, leaving Lina responsible for Jonas. He becomes gravely ill, and Lina herself is weakened almost beyond movement. She nevertheless continues to write and draw, preserving names and experiences that the authorities would prefer to disappear. Dr. Samodurov eventually arrives, recognizes the scale of the disaster, and organizes treatment and additional provisions. His intervention saves Lina, Jonas, and other surviving prisoners, though it cannot undo the deaths or return them home. An epilogue set in Lithuania in 1995 shows workers finding a jar of documents Lina buried after her eventual return. Her account confirms that she and Jonas endured the deportation and that Andrius also survived. The discovery allows Lina's private record to bear witness decades after the Soviet state tried to erase the victims' stories.

characters.description: FitzChivalry Farseer, lately acknowledged as a prince of the Six Duchies and no longer interested in being one. He believes his younger daughter was murdered, he has a hand full of Silver that unmakes whatever it touches unprotected, and he is travelling south with one purpose: to destroy the Servants of Clerres entirely. He is past fifty, damaged by years of Skill use, and better at killing than at anything else he has ever been asked to do.
characters.name: FitzChivalry Farseer

characters.description: Fitz and Molly's younger daughter, about ten years old and small for far less than that, stranded thousands of miles from home in an Elderling city after months lost inside the Skill-pillars. She dreams true, writes everything down, and has survived captivity by being underestimated. Her captors believe she is the awaited one of their prophecies.
characters.name: Bee

characters.description: The White Prophet, healed in body but still blind, travelling south in disguise with Fitz. He grew up inside Clerres, knows its walls, its people and its habits, and wants every one of them dead. He is also keeping things from Fitz, as he always has.
characters.name: The Fool

characters.description: Chade's acknowledged son, a scribe and swordsman of moderate talent who failed to protect Withywoods and has come along to make up for it. He is loyal, unlucky and out of his element on every leg of the journey.
characters.name: FitzVigilant

characters.description: Chade's apprentice, trained in poisons, disguise and quiet violence, who has spent years being taken for a boy and finds it useful. Young, quick and entirely at home in a conspiracy.
characters.name: Spark

characters.description: The Withywoods stable boy who survived the raid, attached himself to Fitz's household and refuses to be sent home. He is the only member of the party who never stopped believing Bee might be alive.
characters.name: Perseverance

characters.description: The Servant who led the raid on Withywoods, stranded far from Clerres with her prize and her prophecy and very little else. Her certainty has survived being lost in the Skill-pillars, and she still intends to deliver Bee to the order that raised her.
characters.name: Dwalia

characters.description: The pale Servant whose fog can make people forget what they are looking at and believe what he wants them to believe. He is powerful, childlike and desperate to be wanted, and Bee has learned exactly where those two things meet.
characters.name: Vindeliar

characters.description: An Elderling and the effective ruler of Kelsingra, once a Bingtown Trader's daughter. She takes in a starving foreign child and a party of strangers who came out of a Skill-pillar and begins working out which of them are prisoners and which are jailers.
characters.name: Malta Khuprus

characters.description: A liveship with a hacked-off face and a violent history, built of wizardwood that was never wood at all. He has capsized, killed crews, been abandoned on a beach and been salvaged, and he is not one person: there is more than one mind in his timbers, and all of them remember being something other than a ship.
characters.name: Paragon

characters.description: A Bingtown Trader's daughter who spent her youth fighting for the right to sail her family's liveship and has been at sea ever since. Blunt, seasoned and unimpressed by rank, she knows the Fool by an older acquaintance and an older name.
characters.name: Althea Vestrit

characters.description: Captain of the liveship Paragon, a disowned Trader's son who made himself a sailor the hard way. He is Althea's husband and the only man who has ever kept Paragon sailing for long.
characters.name: Brashen Trell

characters.description: The son of the pirate king Kennit and the Pirate Isles' reigning queen, handsome, headstrong and deeply unwilling to inherit a throne he never asked for or a father's reputation he does not admire.
characters.name: Kennitsson

characters.description: Ruler of the Pirate Isles, once a whore aboard a pirate ship and now a queen who governs by force of will. She built a kingdom out of her dead husband's legend and intends her son to keep it.
characters.name: Etta

characters.description: The ruling council of Clerres: a handful of Servants who own a walled island fortress, a school, a breeding programme for prophets, and a trade in selling futures to anyone who can pay. They are old, comfortable, and accustomed to being obeyed by everyone within their walls.
characters.name: The Four

characters.description: A dark-skinned man who was a White Prophet in an age long past, and who went south with the Fool when both of them left the Six Duchies. He has been at Clerres a long time and not by choice.
characters.name: Prilkop

recaps.ending: Clerres is destroyed. Fitz poisons, burns and cuts his way through the fortress, the Four are killed, the school and its records go up, and Dwalia and Vindeliar both die there. Bee is found alive, and father and daughter are reunited in the ruins of the place that took her. Prilkop is freed. Paragon keeps his side of the bargain, carries the survivors clear, and is then allowed to become what his timbers always were, separating into dragons and leaving the sea. The party comes home the long way, by liveship to Bingtown and up the Rain Wild River, and Bee is acknowledged as a Farseer, a princess of the Six Duchies in her own right. Fitz does not recover. The Silver, the Skill and the wounds he took at Clerres have used him up, and he is dying by inches; the Fool, who has spent his life spending Fitz, cannot mend him this time. Fitz goes to the Mountain Kingdom, to the quarry where Verity carved his dragon, and gives himself to the stone as the Skilled have always been able to do, pouring his memories and his self into it and finding his wolf waiting there. Bee goes home to Withywoods with the Fool, who stays to raise her, and with Nettle, Riddle, Lant, Spark and Perseverance around her. The Servants are finished, the prophecies they farmed are over, and Bee is left with her father's journals, her own dreams, and a wolf in the woods.
recaps.in_short: Believing Bee dead, Fitz sails south with the Fool, Lant, Spark and Perseverance to destroy the Servants of Clerres, taking passage on the mad liveship Paragon with Althea and Brashen Trell. Bee, meanwhile, is alive: recovered at Kelsingra among the Elderlings, then dragged away again by Dwalia and shipped across the world to Clerres, where the Servants examine her as the fulfilment of their prophecies. Fitz's party crosses the Pirate Isles and the southern sea, Paragon bargaining for a future of his own in exchange for the voyage, and reaches the island fortress. Fitz and the Fool go in and take it apart: poison, fire and murder, the ruling Four killed, the school destroyed, Dwalia and Vindeliar dead. In the ruins Fitz finds Bee alive. Paragon carries them clear and is released to become dragons; the survivors sail home by way of Bingtown and the Rain Wild River, and Bee is acknowledged as a Farseer princess. But Fitz is dying of what the Silver and the Skill and Clerres cost him. He goes to the Mountain quarry where Verity carved his dragon, gives his memories and himself into the stone, and finds his wolf there. Bee goes home to Withywoods with the Fool to raise her.

recaps.text: Previously: FitzChivalry Farseer, royal bastard, assassin and Skill user, was left for dead by the usurper Regal, survived by hiding his mind in his wolf Nighteyes, and let the world bury him; Molly married the stablemaster Burrich and raised Fitz's daughter Nettle as Burrich's own. Guided by the Fool, the White Prophet who named him Catalyst, he helped end the Red Ship war. In the Tawny Man trilogy he returned secretly to court, and on the ice island of Aslevjal the Fool was tortured to death by the Pale Woman and brought back by Fitz through the Skill; the dragon Icefyre was freed and dragons returned to the world. The Fool then left the Six Duchies for the south with Prilkop, an older White Prophet. Fitz married Molly at last and lived twenty quiet years at Withywoods. In Fool's Assassin Molly bore a late, tiny daughter, Bee, who seemed simple and was in fact brilliant and prophetic, and then died; and the Fool returned to Buckkeep blinded and broken by the Servants of Clerres, the order that bred him, warning of an unexpected son they hunted. While Fitz tended him, Servants and Chalcedean mercenaries raided Withywoods behind a fog that erased memory and carried Bee off. In Fool's Quest Fitz healed the Fool with Silver from Chade's secret store, silvering his own hand, then hunted the raiders across the kingdom and destroyed their camp, rescuing Shine but arriving moments after Dwalia took Bee into a Skill-pillar. Convinced his daughter was dead, he was publicly acknowledged as Prince FitzChivalry Farseer and set out south with the Fool, Lant, Spark and Perseverance to annihilate Clerres. Bee, lost inside the pillars for months, emerged alive at Kelsingra, the Elderling city on the Rain Wild River, still a prisoner of Dwalia and still the Shaysim of the Servants' prophecies, with no one who loved her knowing she lived.

Bee is nursed back from starvation at Kelsingra among Elderlings and dragons, a world she knows only from books. Malta Khuprus works out quickly that the child who fell out of a Skill-pillar is not a member of the party that came with her, and that the pale strangers are her jailers, but Vindeliar's fog makes the truth slippery for everyone around him. Far to the north, Fitz's party travels south with a Silver-gloved hand and a plan that is not really a plan: get to Clerres, kill everyone, and do not expect to return. Fitz's Silver touch is a weapon he cannot control, capable of unmaking whatever it touches, and it is also slowly killing him.

Bee is taken out of Kelsingra again. Dwalia gets her away downriver, and the child who was almost safe is back in the hands of the order that stole her, being carried through the Rain Wilds toward the sea and the long voyage to Clerres. She keeps writing, keeps watching, and keeps working on Vindeliar, the only crack in her captors' arrangements. Fitz's party comes down through the Mountains and out to the coast, where the world grows unfamiliar: dragons in the sky, liveships in the harbours, and southern politics that owe the Six Duchies nothing. The distance between father and daughter narrows and neither of them knows it.

At Bingtown the party takes passage on the liveship Paragon, captained by Brashen Trell and sailed by Althea Vestrit, with the pirate heir Kennitsson aboard. The Fool travels openly as Amber, a woman these people knew years ago and remember with mixed feelings, and Fitz becomes her servant again, which suits neither of them. Paragon is not a stable vessel: he is mad, violent, and made from wizardwood that holds more than one mind, none of which was ever human. He agrees to carry them across the southern sea, but on his own terms, and the bargain he strikes is about what he is to be allowed to become when the voyage is over.

The voyage runs through the Pirate Isles, where Etta rules the kingdom her dead husband built and where her son's future is decided over his objections, and out into open water among sea serpents and the ships that hunt them. Aboard Paragon the party rubs against a crew that did not sign on for an assassination, and Amber's secrets and Fitz's temper both cost them. Bee, on another ship on another route, is shipped south as cargo, sustained by her own stubbornness and by the hold she has quietly taken on Vindeliar. Both journeys converge on the same island.

Bee reaches Clerres and is delivered to the Servants, who have waited a long time for the child their prophecies promised. What they do with her is examination rather than ceremony: she is caged, questioned, catalogued and mined for dreams, and she learns what the order actually is, a walled school that breeds prophets, farms their visions, and sells futures to anyone rich enough to buy one. Fitz and Amber arrive at the island and begin scouting a fortress Amber grew up inside, buying information, bribing where they can, and finding that the place is far better defended and far more populous than a vengeance party of five can handle.

The reconnaissance goes wrong. Clerres notices strangers asking questions, the harbour stops being safe, and the party's cover comes apart in accusations and closed gates. Amber's plans and Fitz's plans turn out not to be the same plans, and the cost of that lands on the people who came along out of loyalty. Inside the walls, Bee is one prisoner among many, and the Servants' internal rivalries prove as dangerous to her as their intentions. Prilkop, the White Prophet who went south with the Fool decades ago, is found to be held there too. The party has to get inside a fortress that is now expecting them.

They get in, and Fitz does what he was trained for on a scale nobody asked for. Poison goes into the food and drink of an entire fortress, fires are set, and the assassin the Six Duchies made forty years ago works through Clerres room by room. The Four are confronted and killed, the school's records and its stores of dreams burn, and the order that has been selling the future for generations is destroyed in a night. It is not a clean operation and Fitz does not try to make it one; a great many people die who were never anything but the Servants' property.

In the wreckage Fitz finds Bee alive, and the death he has been avenging for a year turns out never to have happened. Dwalia and Vindeliar both die at Clerres. Prilkop is freed. The survivors fight their way back to the harbour, and Paragon keeps his side of the bargain: he carries them clear, and is then released to become what his timbers always were, separating into dragons and leaving the sea for the sky. Fitz, however, is failing. Between the Silver, the Skill and what Clerres cost him physically, he is being consumed, and neither the Fool nor his own coterie can stop it.

The long way home runs by liveship to Bingtown and up the Rain Wild River, past Kelsingra and its dragons, and back toward the Six Duchies. Bee, who spent a year as a prisoner and a prophecy, is acknowledged as a Farseer and a princess of the realm in her own right, with Nettle, Riddle, Lant, Spark and Perseverance around her. Fitz spends the journey dying, held together by the Skill and by people who will not let go of him, and knowing perfectly well what is happening. He puts his affairs in order and tells his daughter what he can while he can still do it.

Fitz goes to the Mountain Kingdom, to the quarry where Verity carved his dragon out of memory-stone, and does what the Skilled have always been able to do at the end: he gives himself to the stone, pouring his memories, his self and his long life into it rather than simply stopping. Nighteyes is waiting there, and what he becomes is neither a man nor a ghost but something with a wolf's heart in it. Bee goes home to Withywoods with the Fool, who stays to raise her, and inherits her father's journals, her mother's house and her own true dreams. The Servants are finished and their prophecies with them; the White Prophet's work is over; and in the woods around Bee's home there is a wolf.

characters.description: The Farseer bastard, officially dead and buried. He survived Regal's dungeons by retreating into his wolf as his body died, and he has been coaxed back into it over a winter by Burrich and Chade. He is half-wild, easier as a wolf than as a man, with a body ruined by torture and poison and a memory full of gaps. Nothing binds him to the crown any more: the king he swore to is dead, the prince he served is believed dead, and the woman he loved is gone. What he has instead is a single fixed intention, to find Regal and kill him.
characters.name: FitzChivalry Farseer

characters.description: The wolf Fitz bought caged in Buckkeep Town and bonded with through the Wit. He is now full-grown and the bond is total: they share senses, thoughts and, for a time, a body. He is blunt, sardonic and impatient with human tangles, wanting only a pack, a hunt and a place to sleep, and he stays because Fitz is his pack, not because he approves of anything Fitz intends to do.
characters.name: Nighteyes

characters.description: Buckkeep's former stablemaster, who dug Fitz out of his grave and spent the winter dragging him back into a man's shape. Driven out of Buckkeep by Regal's men, lamed, jobless and drinking, he has kept Fitz alive at enormous cost and expects to be obeyed for it. He believes Fitz should go to Kettricken and the Mountains rather than after Regal, and the disagreement is bitter.
characters.name: Burrich

characters.description: The old assassin who trained Fitz, now out of the walls of Buckkeep and living rough, running what is left of a loyalist network for a queen who is over the mountains and a king everyone believes dead. He is exhausted and grimly practical, and he too thinks Fitz should serve the Farseers rather than his own grudge.
characters.name: Chade Fallstar

characters.description: The chandler's daughter Fitz grew up loving, who left Buckkeep without telling him where she was going. She believes him dead, along with everyone else. She exists in this book first as the life Fitz did not get to have.
characters.name: Molly

characters.description: Chivalry's widow, who buried Fitz and grieves him, and who holds Buckkeep Town and its defences together with almost no money and no authority while the crown sits inland at Tradeford. Scattered and stubborn as ever, she turns out to be formidable when there is nobody else left to do the work.
characters.name: Lady Patience

characters.description: The youngest Farseer, now crowned king. He has moved the court inland to Tradeford, stripped Buckkeep of everything portable and left the coastal duchies to defend themselves against the Red Ships. He rules through a Skill coterie of his own, has made the Wit a capital crime and hunts those who carry it, and he had Fitz tortured and condemned.
characters.name: King Regal

characters.description: A travelling minstrel, young, ambitious and short of patrons, working the roads between the coast and the inland duchies. She is quick, unsentimental and entirely clear about what she wants: to witness an event worth a song and so make her name. She recognizes more about her fellow traveller than is comfortable and treats the knowledge as an opportunity.
characters.name: Starling Birdsong

characters.description: An old woman travelling with a party of pilgrims bound for the Mountain Kingdom, small, dry and blunt, who passes the miles at a stone game few people can play well. She is sharper than her years suggest, asks questions that are far too well aimed, and clearly understands things about magic that an ordinary devout old woman would have no way of knowing.
characters.name: Kettle

characters.description: Queen of the Six Duchies in exile, back in her father's country and mourning both her husband and the child she lost. She holds herself to the Mountain idea of the ruler as Sacrifice and is preparing to go herself in search of Verity, on almost no evidence and with almost no help, because nobody else will.
characters.name: Kettricken

characters.description: The former court jester, who fled Buckkeep with Kettricken and lives in the Mountain Kingdom carving wood and keeping the queen company. Away from Buckkeep the mockery is thinner and the seriousness underneath it plainer: the Fool speaks of being a White Prophet, sent to turn the world onto a better course, and of Fitz as the Catalyst whose choices do the turning. Fiercely attached to Fitz and grieved at having believed him dead.
characters.name: The Fool

characters.description: The most able of the Skill coterie Galen trained, now the chief instrument of Regal's rule. Patient and quiet, he hunts Fitz through the Skill itself, reaching for him whenever Fitz's guard slips, and he is far stronger in the magic than Fitz has ever been.
characters.name: Will

characters.description: The rightful King of the Six Duchies, missing for over a year beyond the Mountain Kingdom. He reaches Fitz through the Skill in brief, overwhelming contacts carrying a single command, to come to him. What is left of the plain, dutiful soldier who rode out of Buckkeep is a question the journey is undertaken to answer.
characters.name: Verity Farseer

characters.description: A small daughter born to Molly, being raised in a cottage far from Buckkeep. Fitz learns of her existence through the Skill, long after the fact and from a distance, and can do nothing about it.
characters.name: Nettle

recaps.ending: Verity finishes his dragon by pouring the last of himself into it, and the black stone rises as a living creature carrying him. Kettle gives herself to the unfinished dragon she has spent her life owing a debt to, and other members of the party pay their own prices. Fitz kills Will, taking the coterie's Skill knowledge as he does it, and then reaches into Regal's mind and rewrites him, binding him to serve Queen Kettricken and stripping out his hatred of Fitz entirely, which ends the civil war without another battle. Fitz then wakes the old stone dragons sleeping in the Six Duchies by feeding them memories of his own, and the dragons drive the Red Ships from the coast and end the raiding war. Kettricken returns to Buckkeep as reigning queen, carrying Verity's heir, with Chade and Patience to help her rebuild a stripped and half-ruined kingdom. Verity does not come back as a man. Fitz, still officially dead, makes the choice the whole book has been pushing him towards and stays dead: Molly has a life with Burrich and a daughter who calls Burrich father, and Fitz will not walk into it and break it. He parts from the Fool, keeps Nighteyes, and disappears to a quiet place to write the histories of the war nobody knows he fought. The Farseer line is secure, the coast is free, and the man who bought all of it has given up every claim on his own name.
recaps.in_short: Fitz comes back from the grave half a wolf and spends a winter being coaxed into a man again by Burrich and Chade, then leaves them both to go inland and kill Regal. The attempt fails, and in the middle of it Verity reaches him through the Skill with a single overriding command, to come to him. Compelled, Fitz travels to the Mountain Kingdom with the minstrel Starling and an old pilgrim woman, Kettle, who knows far more about the Skill than she admits, and finds Kettricken and the Fool. The party takes the ancient Skill road beyond the mountains and finds Verity in a stone quarry, carving a dragon and pouring his life into it: the Elderlings of legend are stone dragons, quickened by the people who make them. Through the Skill Fitz sees that Molly is living with Burrich and has borne his daughter, and gives them up.
